clinicalPearls: S. pneumoniae can infect nearly any tissue; the four most common syndromes are otitis media, pneumonia, bacteraemia, and meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1191).

There is no pathognomonic presentation of pneumococcal disease, and a microbiologically confirmed diagnosis is made in only a minority of cases, so empirical therapy covering S. pneumoniae is often indicated (Harrison 22e p.1191).

In the elderly, pneumococcal pneumonia may present non-specifically with confusion or malaise without fever or cough; a high index of suspicion is required because delayed treatment leads to rapid, severe deterioration (Harrison 22e p.1192).

Pneumococcal pneumonia can mimic an acute abdomen (upper abdominal pain from diaphragmatic pleural involvement); clinicians should remember to keep this non-abdominal process in the differential (Harrison 22e p.1192).

Now that H. influenzae type b vaccine is in routine childhood use, S. pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the most common bacterial causes of meningitis in both adults and children (Harrison 22e p.1193).

Pneumococcal meningitis can be a primary presentation or a complication of skull fracture, otitis media, mastoiditis, or bacteraemia; most cases arise from haematogenous spread rather than direct extension (Harrison 22e p.1191, 1193).

A positive urinary pneumococcal antigen test is useful for etiologic attribution in adults (low nasopharyngeal colonization) but is generally uninformative in children and in high-colonization low-income settings (Harrison 22e p.1192-1193).
Most pneumococcal pneumonia is non-bacteraemic; only ~5-20% of cases are accompanied by bacteraemia, and blood cultures are positive in fewer than 30% of cases (Harrison 22e p.1190, 1192).

Empyema is the most common focal complication of pneumococcal pneumonia (<5% of cases); pleural fluid with frank pus, visible bacteria, or pH <=7.1 indicates empyema and demands complete drainage (Harrison 22e p.1192).
harrison.pathophysiology: Pneumococci are encapsulated gram-positive diplococci that colonise the human nasopharynx from an early age; colonisation is common while disease is rare. All pneumococcal infection ultimately stems from nasopharyngeal acquisition. The anti-phagocytic polysaccharide capsule is the key virulence determinant, resisting complement deposition in the absence of type-specific antibody. The organism dynamically modulates capsule expression: it downregulates capsule in the nasopharynx (rough colonies) to evade immune recognition and upregulates it on tissue invasion (smooth colonies). From the nasopharynx, organisms spread haematogenously to distant sites (brain, joints, bone, peritoneum) or locally to mucosal surfaces (otitis media, pneumonia). Intercurrent viral respiratory infection increases susceptibility by upregulating epithelial adhesion factors, permitting adhesion via surface adhesins (PsaA, PspA, CbpA/PspC, pneumolysin, neuraminidases). Disease pathology is driven by host inflammation: cell-wall teichoic acids and peptidoglycan induce IL-1, IL-6, and TNF and activate the alternative complement pathway, and pneumolysin drives proinflammatory cytokine release. Host defence depends on intact respiratory epithelium, the cough reflex and mucociliary escalator, splenic function, complement, neutrophils/macrophages, CRP binding of cell-wall phosphorylcholine, and TLR2/TLR4 recognition, together with acquired anticapsular IgG (Harrison 22e p.1190-1191).
additionalDifferentials: Heart failure with atypical pulmonary oedema
Cholecystitis, appendicitis, perforated peptic ulcer, or subphrenic abscess (when abdominal symptoms predominate)
infectionMimics: Viral lower respiratory tract infection / viral pneumonia
Pneumonia due to H. influenzae, K. pneumoniae, or S. aureus
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts
Other bacterial pyogenic meningitis (e.g., N. meningitidis), clinically indistinguishable from pneumococcal meningitis
nonInfectiousMimics: Heart failure with atypical pulmonary oedema
Lung cancer (can produce round/spherical consolidation mimicking pneumococcal round pneumonia)
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiography (lobar/segmental consolidation; >1 lobe in ~30%; infiltrate may be absent early or with dehydration)
Blood cultures (positive in <30% of pneumococcal pneumonia)
Gram's stain and culture of high-quality sputum (mainstay of adult diagnosis; yield depends on specimen quality and prior antibiotics)
Urinary pneumococcal antigen assay (cell-wall polysaccharide; serotype-specific quantitative assays for up to 24 serotypes emerging)
CSF examination for meningitis: turbidity, elevated protein, elevated WBC, reduced glucose, plus Gram's stain, culture, antigen testing, or PCR
Pleural fluid analysis (pus, microscopy, pH) when effusion present
Sterile aspiration/culture (and capsular antigen or PCR) of fluid from the infected site for other invasive syndromes; lung tissue pathology is the gold standard for pneumonia
redFlags: Asplenia or splenic dysfunction (e.g., sickle cell disease) confers risk of overwhelming, fulminant pneumococcal sepsis
Leukopenia in pneumococcal pneumonia (<10% of cases) is a poor prognostic sign associated with fatal outcome
Hypotension and signs of severe pneumonia/sepsis at presentation predict higher case-fatality
Meningitis features: altered consciousness, seizures, stiff neck, signs of raised intracranial pressure (bradycardia, hypertension), cranial nerve palsies
In children: inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy, or severe malnutrition signify very severe disease warranting immediate antibiotics and referral
Pleural effusion with persistent fever/leukocytosis after 4-5 days of appropriate therapy suggests empyema
harrison.prognosis: Case-fatality varies with age, comorbidity, disease severity at presentation, and access to care. For pneumococcal pneumonia, CFR ranges from <5% in hospitalised patients aged 18-44 to >12% in those over 65, even with timely management; severity at presentation (rather than the presence of bacteraemia) drives mortality, and early deaths reflect a rapidly progressive cascade that often unfolds irrespective of antibiotic administration. Pneumococcal meningitis carries a mortality of ~20%, and up to 50% of survivors have acute or chronic sequelae (deafness, hydrocephalus, and cognitive impairment in children; diffuse brain swelling, subarachnoid bleeding, hydrocephalus, cerebrovascular complications, and hearing loss in adults) (Harrison 22e p.1190, 1193).
pitfalls: Treating an apparent acute abdomen while overlooking pneumococcal lower-lobe pneumonia causing referred abdominal pain (Harrison 22e p.1192).
Relying on a normal early chest radiograph to exclude pneumonia; an infiltrate may be absent early or with dehydration and appear after rehydration (Harrison 22e p.1192).
Over-interpreting a positive urinary pneumococcal antigen in children or in high-colonization settings, where it does not reliably attribute etiology (Harrison 22e p.1192-1193).
Diagnosing otitis media from tympanic-membrane redness alone, which is insufficient (Harrison 22e p.1193).
Attributing round/spherical consolidation solely to pneumococcus without considering other causes, especially cancer (Harrison 22e p.1192).

Assuming PPSV23 reliably prevents non-bacteraemic pneumococcal pneumonia, particularly in the elderly and immunodeficient, where effectiveness is reduced and protection wanes after ~5 years (Harrison 22e p.1194).
harrison.severityClassification: Pneumococcal syndromes are classified as invasive (a normally sterile site is infected or bacteraemia is present, e.g., bacteraemic pneumonia, meningitis, bacteraemia) versus noninvasive (contiguous spread, e.g., otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis); whether non-bacteraemic pneumonia counts as invasive is debated. In children, WHO IMCI algorithms stratify illness by danger signs (very severe disease: inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy, severe malnutrition) and by cough with tachypnoea plus lower chest-wall indrawing to guide antibiotics and referral; no equivalent validated algorithm exists for adults (Harrison 22e p.1191).
